title: Education Myatt, Mary Overrated and Underrated No. 196
author: Myatt, Mary
summary: Myatt argues that schemes of work are systematically structured to prioritize coverage over depth, sending students an implicit message: the content matters more than your thinking about it. She illustrates depth with a Year 7 RE lesson where the teacher spent three lessons on covenant in Judaism -- not because students were struggling but because they were thinking, and by the third lesson they were using precise vocabulary (sacred, binding, unconditional) that signaled genuine understanding. The core argument: racing through schemes of work is overrated; staying with one idea until pupils genuinely understand it is underrated.
points: * Coverage is not rigour -- depth is: schemes of work built around racing to cover the unit pressure teachers to leave understanding behind, and the implicit message to students is that the content matters more than their thinking. * Depth is not slower, it is richer: staying with one concept across multiple lessons allows students to notice things on day three that they missed on day one. * The permission question for school leaders: what would change if schemes of work explicitly allowed teachers to stay longer with the ideas that matter most? * Precise vocabulary as evidence of understanding: students using words like 'sacred,' 'binding,' and 'unconditional' with precision after three lessons on covenant differentiates genuine understanding from surface familiarity. * When a teacher stays with an idea, students receive a different message: 'your understanding is worth the time,' and that message has its own pedagogical effect.
quotes: Overrated: Racing through schemes of work. Underrated: Staying with one idea until pupils genuinely understand it.

I watched a Year 7 RE lesson recently where the teacher did something unusual. She stayed with the concept of covenant in Judaism for three lessons. Not because pupils were struggling. Because they were thinking.
By the third lesson, pupils were noticing things they had missed on day one. The weight of mutual obligation. The difference between a contract and a covenant.
They were using words like 'sacred,' 'binding,' and 'unconditional' with precision. This is what depth looks like. Not slower. Richer.
But our schemes of work often work against this. They are built around coverage: move on, tick off, get through. The pressure to finish the unit becomes the pressure to leave understanding behind.
When we rush, pupils receive a message: the content matters more than your thinking about it. When we stay, they receive a different message: your understanding is worth the time.
Coverage is not rigour, depth is. What would change if your schemes of work gave teachers permission to stay longer with the ideas that matter most?
